title: Myth that losing semen makes you weak
answer: Some people believe that ejaculating, wet dreams or masturbation drain a man's strength, blood or brain power. This is a myth. The body makes new sperm and semen all the time, and releasing semen does not cause weakness, illness, back pain or infertility. Feeling tired afterwards is normal and passes quickly. If you feel weak all the time, there is another cause, so see a health worker.

title: Blood after first sex
answer: Some girls and women notice a little bleeding the first time they have vaginal sex, and many do not. A small amount of light bleeding that stops within a day or so is usually not serious. Heavy bleeding, bleeding that does not stop, strong pain, fever or bad-smelling discharge need care: go to a health center. If the sex was not your choice, you deserve care and support; please go to a health facility quickly.

title: No bleeding after first sex
answer: Many girls and women do not bleed the first time they have sex. The hymen is a thin, stretchy tissue that differs from person to person, and it can stretch through sport, daily activity or simply be naturally open. No bleeding does not mean someone has had sex before. Bleeding is not a test of virginity, and nobody can tell your sexual history by looking at your body.

title: Feeling nervous about first sex
answer: It is normal to feel nervous about having sex for the first time. Ask yourself if you truly feel ready, or if you feel pushed. You can always wait or change your mind, even at the last minute. If you decide to go ahead, talk with your partner first, plan protection against pregnancy and infections, and choose a time and place where you feel safe and respected. Never use alcohol to calm nerves.

title: Bleeding after sex
answer: Bleeding after sex that is not your first time, or that happens again and again, should be checked. It can be caused by dryness, small tears, infections including STIs, changes on the cervix, or bleeding linked to contraception. Most causes can be treated, but some need early care. Please see a nurse or health worker at the health center, especially if you also have pain, unusual discharge or bleeding between periods.

title: Can having sex often harm you
answer: For healthy adults, having sex often is not harmful by itself, as long as both partners want it, it is comfortable, and you protect yourselves against infections and unplanned pregnancy. Soreness, pain, burning, bleeding or unusual discharge are signs to rest and see a health worker. Having many partners increases the risk of infections. Sex should never feel forced or a duty.

title: Testicle ache after arousal
answer: Some boys and men feel a dull ache or heaviness in the testicles after being sexually aroused for a long time without ejaculating. This happens because extra blood flows to the area. It is uncomfortable but harmless and goes away on its own within a short time. It is never a reason to pressure anyone into sex. Severe or sudden pain, swelling or pain that lasts needs a health worker.

title: Medicines that affect sexual function
answer: Some medicines, including some for depression, blood pressure, epilepsy and other long-term conditions, can affect desire, erections, wetness or climax for some people. If you notice changes after starting a medicine, do not stop it on your own, because that can be dangerous. Talk to the health worker who prescribed it. There are often other options or ways to manage the side effect.

title: Vaginal steaming
answer: Vaginal steaming means sitting over hot water, sometimes with herbs, to 'clean' or 'tighten' the vagina. There is no evidence that it cleans, tightens or improves fertility. title: Feminine sprays and perfumes on the genitals
answer: Perfumes, body sprays, deodorants, scented powders and 'feminine fresheners' are not needed on the genitals. They can irritate the delicate skin, cause itching, burning or allergic rashes, and upset the natural balance of the vagina, making infections more likely. A mild natural smell is normal. Washing the outside daily with clean water is enough. A strong or fishy smell needs a health check, not perfume.

title: Tight and synthetic underwear
answer: Underwear that is very tight or made of synthetic material like nylon traps heat and sweat. This can cause rubbing, rashes, and make yeast and other infections more likely in girls. In boys, tight underwear and trousers keep the testicles warm, which may slightly lower sperm quality. Cotton underwear that fits comfortably lets the skin breathe. Change it daily and when wet with sweat.

title: Wiping front to back
answer: Girls and women should wipe from front to back after using the toilet, from the vagina towards the anus. Wiping the other way can carry germs from the bottom to the urinary opening and vagina, causing urine infections and other infections. Use clean toilet paper or water and wash hands afterwards. Signs of a urine infection include burning when urinating and needing to go often; see a health worker if this happens.

title: Sleeping without underwear
answer: Sleeping without underwear, or in loose cotton clothes, is healthy for most people. It lets the genital area stay dry and breathe, which can help prevent sweat rashes and yeast infections. If you prefer to wear underwear at night, choose clean, loose cotton. During your period, wear underwear with a pad. Clean bedsheets regularly. It is a personal choice; both options are fine.

title: Heat and sperm health
answer: Testicles hang outside the body because sperm develop best slightly below body temperature. Frequent heat, such as very tight trousers, long hot baths, sitting for many hours, or laptops resting on the lap, can temporarily lower sperm quality. This usually recovers once the heat is reduced. Wearing loose underwear and taking breaks from sitting helps. If you have concerns about fertility, see a health worker.

title: Breast pain not linked to periods
answer: Breast pain at times other than before your period is common and is usually not a sign of cancer. It can come from a poorly fitting bra, exercise, muscle strain in the chest, injury, growth, or some hormonal contraception. A supportive bra and rest may help. title: Breast cancer in young women
answer: Breast cancer is rare in teenagers and uncommon in young women, though it can happen. Most breast lumps and pains at a young age are not cancer. Still, it is good to know how your breasts normally look and feel and to report changes, such as a new lump, skin dimpling, a nipple turning inward, bloody discharge or a sore that does not heal. Early checks save lives, so see a health worker if worried.

title: Mother or relative with breast cancer
answer: If your mother, sister or another close relative had breast cancer, especially at a young age, your own risk may be a bit higher, but most people with a relative who had it never get it. title: Testicular self-examination
answer: Checking your testicles once a month helps you know what is normal. The best time is during or after a warm bath when the skin is relaxed. Gently roll each testicle between your thumb and fingers. It should feel smooth and firm. The soft tube at the back (the epididymis) is normal. Look for lumps, swelling, hardness or changes in size. If you notice anything new, see a health worker.

answer: A new lump, hard area or swelling on a testicle should always be checked by a health worker, even if it does not hurt. title: Sudden testicle pain
answer: Sudden, severe pain in a testicle, especially with swelling, nausea or vomiting, can mean the testicle has twisted (testicular torsion). title: Mother with cervical cancer: am I at risk
answer: Cervical cancer is mostly caused by long-lasting infection with HPV, a virus passed through sexual contact, not by genes passed from mother to child. You can protect yourself by getting the HPV vaccine, delaying sex, using condoms, not smoking, and going for cervical screening when you reach the recommended age. title: What the prostate is
answer: The prostate is a small gland, about the size of a walnut, found only in men. It sits below the bladder and surrounds the tube that carries urine out of the body. It makes some of the fluid in semen that helps sperm move and stay healthy. The prostate often grows bigger as men get older, which can cause problems with urinating in later life.

title: Prostate cancer basics for your father
answer: Prostate cancer is a common cancer in older men, mostly after age 50. Early on it often has no signs. Later signs can include trouble urinating, a weak flow, blood in urine or semen, and pain in the back or hips, though these can also have other causes. Men in their 50s, or earlier if a close relative had it, should talk to a health worker about checks. Treatment works best when found early.

title: Father having trouble urinating
answer: Many older men have trouble urinating because the prostate grows bigger with age and presses on the urine tube. Signs include a weak flow, difficulty starting, needing to go often, especially at night, or feeling the bladder is not empty. title: Skipping breakfast
answer: After a night without food, your body and brain need energy. Skipping breakfast can make you tired, unable to concentrate in class, irritable, and more likely to eat sugary snacks later. A simple breakfast helps, such as porridge (igikoma), sweet potatoes, bread with an egg or groundnut paste, milk, or fruit. title: Sugary drinks and junk food
answer: Soda, sweet juices, sweets, chips and fried snacks taste good but contain a lot of sugar, salt and fat and few nutrients. Having them often can lead to tooth decay, unhealthy weight gain and, over time, diabetes and heart disease. Enjoy them only sometimes. Choose water, milk, fruit, groundnuts and home-cooked food more often. Your body needs real food to grow, learn and stay strong.

answer: Water helps your body control temperature, digest food, keep skin healthy and think clearly. Not drinking enough can cause headaches, tiredness, constipation, dark urine and poor concentration. Drink water regularly through the day, more when it is hot, when you exercise or when you are sick. Light yellow urine is a good sign you are drinking enough. answer: Your teenage years are when bones become strongest, so calcium matters. Good sources include milk, yoghurt (ikivuguto), small fish eaten with bones like isambaza, beans, and dark green leafy vegetables.
